title: Event Sourcing for Agentic Workflows
summary: Agentic workflow state becomes recoverable by recording progress as an append-only log (the goal first, then decision and result entries) and making the in-memory state a fold over it. Three rules carry the design: apply_step/2 updates state only and never starts work, calls a model or sends a message, so replaying the log cannot re-run side effects; record/2 persists before it applies, so the log is always ahead of memory and memory stays rebuildable; and step_id, a workflow-assigned number, replaces node-local make_ref/0. A Registry with unique keys via {:via, Registry, ...} turns single-writer into a guarantee ({:error, {:already_started, pid}}), and {:continue, :rebuild} makes OTP rebuild state in handle_continue/2 before any other message is processed.
source: inbox/articles/Exploring OTP Patterns for Agentic Workflows.md

chunks.content:
# Event Sourcing for Agentic Workflows

Let it crash only works because a supervisor can start a new process in a known good state — but for a workflow that known good state means starting from the beginning, repeating every model decision and every tool call. The fix is to treat the workflow's progress as an append-only log and make the in-memory state a fold over it. Three rules make this work: `apply_step/2` stays free of side effects, `record/2` persists before it applies, and the identifier is a workflow-assigned `step_id` rather than a node-local `make_ref/0`.

chunks.section: If this process dies, what happens to the run?
Rebuilding the state from the log
chunks.content:
## Rebuilding the state from the log

Let’s put that idea into code. Three things change: the workflow gets an id that survives the process, each tool call gets a step id the workflow assigns, and every state change goes through a single function.

```
defstruct [:id, :goal, :model, history: [], pending: %{}, steps: 0, max_steps: 10]

# Only updates the state: no work, no model calls, no messages
defp apply_step({:goal, goal}, state), do: %{state | goal: goal}

defp apply_step({:decision, step_id, call}, state) do
  %{state | pending: Map.put(state.pending, step_id, call), steps: state.steps + 1}
end

defp apply_step({:result, step_id, result}, state) do
  {call, pending} = Map.pop(state.pending, step_id)
  %{state | pending: pending, history: [{call, result} | state.history]}
end
```

Each clause handles one kind of entry from the log. `apply_step/2` never starts work, calls a model, or sends a message. That restriction will matter in a moment.

The owner is still the only one that writes:

```
@impl true
def handle_info({:tool_result, step_id, result}, state)
    when is_map_key(state.pending, step_id) do
  state = record({:result, step_id, result}, state)
  next_step(state)
end

# Each call becomes a decision in the log, with a step id the workflow assigns
defp request(calls, state) do
  Enum.reduce(calls, state, fn call, state ->
    record({:decision, state.steps + 1, call}, state)
  end)
end

# Persist first, then apply
defp record(entry, state) do
  :ok = BlogOtp.Log.append(state.id, entry)
  apply_step(entry, state)
end
```

Notice two things.

The first is `step_id`, which replaces the reference from the previous version. A reference created with `make_ref/0` only identifies something within the running node, and the process waiting for it may be gone after a crash. A step id is just a number the workflow assigns when it records the decision, and it means the same thing to any process that reads the log.

The second is the order inside `record/2`. We write to the log first, then apply the entry to the in-memory state. If the process dies between those two lines, the log is ahead of memory, and memory is the part we know how to rebuild. The other way around, the process could act on a step that no restart would ever see. And if the append fails, the process crashes before acting on anything.

The same rule applies to decisions: they’re recorded before anyone starts the work. In this chapter nobody executes the tools yet, but when someone does, the decision will already be in the log.

This puts a durable write on the owner’s critical path. That’s intentional: we don’t want the workflow to act on a transition it couldn’t recover after a crash.

*In this chapter,* *BlogOtp.Log* *keeps its entries in an ETS table owned by its own process. It survives a workflow crash, but not a node restart. A real implementation would write to disk or a database; the contract, append first and read in order, stays the same.*

Starting a run now means creating its log first:

```
def start(goal, opts \\ []) do
  id = new_id()
  :ok = BlogOtp.Log.append(id, {:goal, goal})

  DynamicSupervisor.start_child(
    BlogOtp.WorkflowSupervisor,
    {__MODULE__, Keyword.put(opts, :id, id)}
  )
end

def start_link(opts) do
  GenServer.start_link(__MODULE__, opts, name: via(Keyword.fetch!(opts, :id)))
end

defp via(id), do: {:via, Registry, {BlogOtp.WorkflowRegistry, id}}
```

The goal is written before the owner exists; from then on, the owner is the only writer. Registering the process under the workflow id in a `Registry` with unique keys turns “only one writer” from an intention into a guarantee: a key points to at most one process, and a second attempt to start an owner for the same run would get `{:error, {:already_started, pid}}`.

Look at what the process is started with: the id, not the goal. When a supervisor restarts a child, it calls the same start function, with the same arguments, from the child’s specification. The id is all a new process needs to find out everything else.

```
@impl true
def init(opts) do
  state = %__MODULE__{
    id: Keyword.fetch!(opts, :id),
    model: Keyword.get(opts, :model, BlogOtp.Model.Scripted),
    max_steps: Keyword.get(opts, :max_steps, 10)
  }

  {:ok, state, {:continue, :rebuild}}
end

@impl true
def handle_continue(:rebuild, state) do
  state =
    state.id
    |> BlogOtp.Log.read()
    |> Enum.reduce(state, &apply_step/2)

  next_step(state)
end
```

When `init/1` returns `{:continue, :rebuild}`, OTP runs `handle_continue/2` before the process receives any other message, so no result can be handled while the state is still being rebuilt.

The same `apply_step/2` that updates the workflow while it runs also rebuilds it after a crash. Now we can see why it had to be free of side effects: replaying the log must not run the tests again. And a new run isn’t a special case either: it’s a log with a single entry, the goal. The fold produces a state with nothing pending, and `next_step/1` asks the model for its first decision.

The state is a fold over the log.

This changes what a restart means. The new process doesn’t need to remember what the old one knew. It only needs to rebuild enough of the workflow to continue from a known point. But careful!
